text: SABSA starts from business attributes and works down. TOGAF starts from a different place entirely — the enterprise architecture practice itself, as a whole. It's maintained by The Open Group, a vendor-neutral industry consortium, and it's the most widely adopted enterprise architecture framework in use today. Understanding where security fits into it — and where it doesn't, by default — is essential once you're working alongside an existing enterprise architecture team.

TOGAF organizes architecture work around four domains, often shortened to BDAT: Business architecture covers strategy and governance; Data architecture covers how information assets are structured and managed; Application architecture covers the systems themselves and how they interact; and Technology architecture covers the hardware, software, and network underneath all of it. Every TOGAF engagement is framed in terms of these four domains.

The engine that drives all of this is the Architecture Development Method, or ADM — a cyclical process with phases lettered A through H, wrapped around central requirements management. Phases A through D move from vision through business, information systems, and technology architecture. E and F group and sequence the resulting changes into work packages. G and H govern implementation and keep the architecture current as things change. It's explicitly not a one-and-done project plan.

Here's the part that catches security architects off guard: there's no dedicated security box on that diagram. Security isn't a fifth BDAT domain. Historically that meant security got reviewed late, after the real decisions were already made. The Open Group's own guidance, the TOGAF Series Guide on Integrating Risk and Security, corrects that by treating security as a cross-cutting concern — addressed inside every single ADM phase, from the vision in Phase A to the compliance checks in Phase G, instead of confined to one spot.

That's exactly why SABSA and TOGAF show up together so often in real practice. TOGAF is a process framework — it tells you how the architecture practice runs. SABSA is a content framework — it tells you what the security architecture should actually contain. Joint guidance from The Open Group and the SABSA Institute shows SABSA's layers and its Business Attributes Profile filling the security content inside each TOGAF ADM phase, so neither framework has to do the other's job.

You've now seen two very different starting points — business-first with SABSA, process-first with TOGAF. Next lesson brings back something you already know from security engineering: CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model. This time you'll use it the way an architect does — as an input to planning the target state, not just as an engineering checklist.
